storyline.arc: It started as an embedded terminal wrapper trying to speak both Claude and OpenCode, then grew session sharing, worktree sandboxes, and a dashboard. Now it runs as a background daemon on three platforms, reconstructs history you never recorded with --backtrace, and ships a learn page with personalized coaching.

chapters.detail: The trigger was simple: after an aGiTrack update, both dashboards just stopped and nobody restarted them. So the daemons got unhooked from the terminal that spawned them (including the Ctrl-G dashboard, which now behaves exactly like `agitrack -d`), and agitrack/update/restart.py swapped its exec-based restart for a spawn-and-verify pattern with rollback. The nice part: a daemon that failed to restart still shows up under `-daemons` and still honours stop commands, instead of vanishing and pretending it was never there.
chapters.summary: Background daemons now stand on their own and try again instead of quietly dying.

thoughts.note: Working out that a failed restart still needs to be visible and stoppable, not silently gone.

thoughts.note: After the dashboards died anyway, they stopped trusting exec and moved to spawn, verify, then roll back if it did not come up.

chapters.detail: The two views were never going to agree while the watermark logic quietly re-exported whole sessions after a lost context, so the fix ran a real experiment first: a dummy repo, a few agent turns with edits, then a line-by-line compare of the token counts in commit messages against what backtrace reported. Once the accounting in collect.py and recovery.py lined up, the backtrace cache turned out to be solving a problem nobody had, so it went, and the intro paragraph in the backtrace log now spells out that the subjects listed are the user prompts for each turn.
chapters.summary: Two dashboards disagreed on token counts until three independent bugs were found and the cache dropped.

thoughts.note: Restart counts could not explain the gap, so they stopped guessing and built a dummy repo to measure both numbers side by side.
thoughts.quote: There were only a few restarts, so that cannot explain such a big difference

thoughts.note: With the counts finally matching, they looked at the backtrace cache and decided it was not earning its keep.
thoughts.quote: I don't think backtrace really needs a cache

chapters.title: Three separate token-counting bugs, and a backtrace cache nobody needed

chapters.detail: Two dashboards on the same repo, same 24 hour window, and the numbers still would not line up. The prompt was blunt about it: find the abnormal commits and either fix or exclude them from the token count. So collect.py and web.py learned to spot the outliers and drop them, and the earlier bad numbers got cleaned up too by rewriting the old commit messages with corrected token counts.
chapters.summary: Even after the token fixes the numbers differed, and the culprit was outlier commits.

thoughts.note: They stopped trusting the filter alone and decided the data itself had bad rows in it.
thoughts.quote: What did you fix. When I run both dashboards on the current repo, I still see a big difference even with the 24 hours filter. The dashboard needs to detect abnormal commits and exclude/fix them in the token count. In addition, such abnormal commits should never happen again.

thoughts.note: Fixing the code was not enough, the wrong numbers were already baked into old commit messages.
thoughts.quote: Please amend the affected commit messages with the correct number of tokens

chapters.title: The two dashboards still disagreed, so abnormal commits got excluded

chapters.detail: The self-update work in agitrack/update/selfupdate.py needed locking because a TUI and a daemon can both decide it's upgrade time at the same moment, and two copies rewriting the same install is nobody's idea of a good day. The other half came from a very ordinary annoyance: paste a few lines into the backend agent's terminal and the embedded line breaks got read as Enter, which then answered aGiTrack's own "new commits?" popup on your behalf. There was also a small round of taste-correction, where self-update went from opt-in to on by default with a config switch for anyone who'd rather not.
chapters.summary: Multi-instance locking so updates don't collide, plus a fix for mangled multi-line pastes into the agent terminal.

thoughts.note: Working out that if both the TUI and the daemon can trigger an update, they need to agree on who goes first.
thoughts.quote: aGiTrack should self-update when it can, which can be triggered by either the TUI or the daemon. There is no need to ask the user for updating the installation itself, although the TUI should not automatically restart to avoid interruptions (the same update restart reminder in the TUI should stay). When multiple aGiTrack instances are running, make sure their self-updates don't clash, so there needs to be some mechanism that only one aGiTrack instance can start a self-update, maybe through a lock mechanism.

thoughts.note: Realizing the terminal can't tell a pasted newline from a real keypress, so the modal has to stop trusting it.
thoughts.quote: When pasting multiple lines into the backend agent's terminal, some line breaks in what is pasted gets detected by aGiTrack as Enter, which unintentionally gets applied to aGiTrack's pop up menu asking users about new commits etc. This should be avoided.

chapters.title: Self-update lands, and pasted line breaks stop vanishing
